2f7bd37e11.q: What specific eye contact and greeting technique should women entrepreneurs use when entering networking rooms to build immediate connections?
2f7bd37e11.a: When you catch eye contact with someone, do not ignore it—step right in and say hello with your name and ask them to tell you about themselves. This breaks the first barrier through eye contact. If you cannot get across the room, at least smile and acknowledge them rather than looking away, because eye contact makes a deep connection right away. When you grab an eye connection, you are engaging right then.

312507998a.q: How long should a woman entrepreneur speak about herself when sharing at a networking table before it becomes counterproductive?
312507998a.a: You should keep your share to around one to two minutes maximum. When someone talks for three minutes or longer at a table, it actually goes against you—everyone gets uncomfortable and wants to move to the next person. Oversharing signals you do not know how to present yourself, you are not aware of the room, and you are caught up in yourself. Talking more will not make people want to buy from you more.

2954ed7927.q: What is the value-focused storytelling approach that Christina Vidovich recommends instead of directly pitching services at networking events?
2954ed7927.a: Instead of talking about yourself, explain a client's journey and transformation. For example, Christina worked with a woman who wanted to become a speaker, helped craft her 10-minute talk, got her on stage, and months later that client launched her own coaching business. This client story explains more than saying verbatim what you do—it demonstrates your value through real results rather than features.

0002ae70a6.q: How should women entrepreneurs recognize and act on red flags in potential business partnerships based on trust instincts?
0002ae70a6.a: If you have hesitation or do not know about partnering with someone, do not do it. Trust your instincts—there is a balance between logic and intuition. If someone is showing warning signals, investigate quickly and do not wait. If a partnership is not benefiting both parties equally, it is okay to say no and have that conversation. Quick decisions prevent problems from escalating into major issues.

5c3ac3cbbe.q: What does Amy recommend about forgiveness and mistake-handling in business relationships where trust and likeability are established?
5c3ac3cbbe.a: People will work with and forgive people they like, know, and trust—if they mess up, the person can apologize and it will be okay. But if they do not like or trust you and you mess up, you usually get fired almost immediately. That likeability, knowledge, and trust foundation is key, even when things happen in the world you cannot control.
